![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14116420/assets/4c38294780ac6d5079b759f39a7dbd4944b1c3c21495245dfd314ec180c0434e.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{curl}\,F=0$
- $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$
- $F$ is irrotational
- $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14116420/assets/979b63f21e56924bd7880f9487cf829089e38cf14d287e70196c7a661e41f97f.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is true, whereas statement II is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

- $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction.

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14116420/assets/f385add60afac473a5734f8c1ed57c6575bada03c9c16b24fed73b200c38e2c5.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (clockwise), our thumb will point into the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points into the screen, in the direction of decreasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(\pi ,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\cdot y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(\pi ,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(\pi ,0)} & =-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)-\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =0-\pi \cdot 1 \\  & =-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,i+(x{y}^{2}+1)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)) \\  & ={y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,\pi /2)} & ={(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $F(x,y)=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j,$ what is the scalar curl of $F?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
